The six steps of dealflow management, in the order the articles lay them out, are sourcing, filtering, diligence, decisions, closing, and follow-up: How VCs Source Deals in Emerging VC, How VCs Filter Dealflow in Emerging VC, Early Stage Diligence in Emerging VC, Decision-making in Emerging VC, Closing Deals in Emerging VC, and How VCs Manage Followup. Reading the titles in sequence was the useful part on its own. Dealflow is the stream of startups arriving at an investor, and I had been treating the whole thing as one activity called finding deals, when only the first sixth of it is finding anything.

The aspect I am least familiar with is filtering, and specifically the split between the first-level and the second-level filter. My honest situation is that I have inflow and no filter. I am an alum of Plug and Play, Grid110, and Material Change, so introductions reach me without much effort on my part, and until now I have handled each one ad hoc: a call, a good conversation, no decision. What I want to develop is a written screen I apply the same way every time, so that a pass is a repeatable decision rather than a mood, and so I can say no quickly and specifically without spending the relationship.

What I learned. A first-level filter is a mechanical screen against the thesis itself, on sector, geography, stage, and valuation range, and it is supposed to be cheap, because its only job is to clear obvious mismatches before they cost anyone a meeting. A second-level filter is where human judgment starts: a focused first call of about thirty minutes, then pre-diligence on market size, customer validation, scalability, and team depth. Three things changed how I will actually work. First, a pass is where you spend relationship capital rather than save it. The Decile article's example is an investor who passes on a company with customer retention under 50% and introduces the founder to a mentor who specializes in churn on the way out, which is the version of no I want to be known for. Second, the scale of it. VC Lab's investment process article puts numbers on the funnel: roughly 500 leads become 100 potential investments, then 50 meetings, 20 in-depth reviews, 10 due diligence processes, 5 term sheets, and 1 investment. Almost all of this job is saying no, so the cost of each no compounds, and Bessemer's Anti-Portfolio, the public list of great companies that firm passed on, is the counterweight: a filter tight enough never to waste a meeting is also tight enough to screen out the outlier. Third, and this is the one I did not expect, the article's closing example is a VC who realizes after twenty second-stage calls that her strongest filter is not financial at all, and that she is really testing for coachability and founder-solution fit. At pre-seed there is no revenue to analyze, so that is not a refinement of the screen, it is the screen. The same article makes the point that a thesis stated in four words turns everyone you meet into a deal scout, which lands for me specifically: if I cannot say my filter in one breath, the three alumni networks I am counting on cannot route deals to me.

Later in the program I want to go deeper on two of the six steps. Decisions, because I want to know how conviction actually gets formed and written down at pre-seed, when the underwriting is almost entirely the founder. And follow-up, which I suspect is the step that separates angels who see the next deal from angels who see one deal. Closing mechanics matter less to me right now, because as an angel writing personal checks I am not negotiating complicated terms yet, but I do live or die on whether founders come back.

Sources I used:

1. https://decilegroup.com/articles/deals-filtering-emerging-vc - first- and second-level filters
2. https://decilegroup.com/articles/deals-sourcing-emerging-vc - where deals actually come from
3. https://govclab.com/2023/06/14/vc-investment-process/ - the 500-to-1 funnel, step by step
4. https://www.bvp.com/anti-portfolio - the cost of a filter that is too tight

My niche is AI that rebuilds human trust: technology that builds bridges, strengthens community bonds, and fosters belonging, backed at pre-seed in the United States. Five companies from that niche that reached a notable exit or a late-stage round:

- Nextdoor, 2021, about $4.3 billion. A private social network organized by physical neighborhood, built so that people who live near each other can actually reach each other; it went public in November 2021 by merging with Khosla Ventures Acquisition Co. II.
- Discord, 2021, about $15 billion. Persistent voice and text communities where groups of people who would otherwise never meet build durable social ties; it reached that valuation in a $500 million round led by Dragoneer in September 2021.
- Patreon, 2021, about $4 billion. A direct membership relationship between creators and the people who value their work, in place of algorithmic distribution; it reached that valuation in a $155 million round led by Tiger Global in April 2021.
- Hive, 2021, about $2 billion. AI content moderation and understanding, sold as an API to the platforms that have to keep abuse, fraud, and synthetic media off their services; it reached that valuation in an $85 million Series D led by Glynn Capital in April 2021.
- Sift, 2021, just over $1 billion. A digital trust and safety platform that uses machine learning to tell real customers apart from fraud without adding friction for the real ones; it raised $50 million led by Insight Partners in April 2021.

Is there enough venture scale in this niche, or do I need to widen it? There is, but the honest answer has a split in it that I did not expect to find. The companies in my niche that reached real scale fall into two groups that barely resemble each other. The community and belonging companies, Nextdoor and Discord and Patreon, got very large, but they are social platforms that added AI later rather than AI companies. The AI-native ones, Hive and Sift, are trust and safety infrastructure sold to enterprises, and they top out around $1 to $4 billion rather than $15 billion. So outcomes exist at both ends, but the specific thing I am looking for, an AI-native company whose product is trust between people rather than fraud scoring for a platform, does not have a finished ten-billion-dollar example yet. I do not read that as a reason to widen the niche. As an angel writing personal checks I do not need a decacorn for the math to work, and the absence of a finished example is closer to a reason to be early than a reason to move. It does sharpen the open question I already had written down, which is whether a trust and belonging filter selects for or against outliers. My read after this exercise is that it does not select against them, but it does select for a slower shape of outcome, and that is a question for when I size a fund rather than a question for the checks I am writing now.

The earliest backers of each, and how those relationships likely formed:

- Nextdoor: Shasta Ventures, seed, October 2011, before the neighborhood-by-neighborhood growth pattern was visible. Benchmark, with Bill Gurley leading, in the $18.6 million round announced July 2012 alongside Greylock Partners and DAG Ventures. The relationship almost certainly predates the company: Nirav Tolia was a repeat founder who had co-founded Epinions, so the seed investors were people who had watched him work before there was anything to evaluate.
- Discord: YouWeb's 9+ incubator at the seed stage, into Hammer and Chisel, the game studio that became Discord. Then Mitch Lasky at Benchmark, who led an $8.2 million round in November 2013, before Discord existed as a product, with Accel and Tencent also in early. Jason Citron had already built and sold OpenFeint to GREE for $104 million in 2011, and Lasky had backed Riot Games, so this was a repeat-founder bet made by investors who knew the category and the person.
- Patreon: a $2.1 million seed in August 2013, co-led by Freestyle Capital and Index Ventures, with Alexis Ohanian among the angels. Jack Conte was a working musician with an audience before he was a founder, which means the problem he was solving was one he could describe from the inside. That is founder-market fit an investor can verify in a single conversation.
- Hive: General Catalyst and 8VC among the earliest institutional backers, with the company starting as a consumer app and pivoting at the end of 2017 to sell the content moderation tooling it had built for itself. The money predates the business that made the company, which is worth noticing: those investors backed a team through a pivot into an entirely different product.
- Sift: Y Combinator, Summer 2011 batch, then a Series A led by Union Square Ventures with Albert Wenger joining the board, and First Round Capital and Max Levchin in early alongside. This is the cleanest accelerator-to-institutional path of the five. The founders were ex-Google engineers, YC was the entry point, and the early institutional investors were people the accelerator put in the room.

What that pattern tells me. Four of the five earliest relationships came from somebody having watched the founder work before there was a company to evaluate: a prior startup, a prior audience, a prior batch. Only one came from a formal program, and even that one worked because the program put the founders in front of investors who would not otherwise have met them. That is exactly the mechanism my own edge runs on, and it is an argument for staying visible inside Plug and Play, Grid110, and Material Change between programs rather than only during them. I got a live confirmation of that this week. I screened all twenty-nine companies Plug and Play Seattle has published across its first three batches, and the strongest one to come out of it, Glacis, took its first money from the AI2 Incubator and from Geoff Ralston's Safe Artificial Intelligence Fund. That is the same incubator-to-institutional path Sift took, running right now, inside one of my own three ecosystems.

[YOUR PARAGRAPH - OUTREACH. Replace this before submitting. Contact at least three sources from the research above and write a couple of sentences on who you contacted, what you said, and any initial responses. Warmest realistic targets, in order: someone in your three ecosystems who overlaps with any of these five companies; an operator at one of the five reachable through a mutual connection; a seed investor working on trust and safety in Seattle.]

I ran my first systematic sourcing pass this week instead of waiting for introductions to arrive. My honest situation going into this sprint was inflow without a filter, so I pointed the filter at a list I could actually enumerate: every company Plug and Play Seattle has published across its first three batches, twenty-nine in all. Plug and Play is one of the three ecosystems I came up through, so this was channel one of my own dealflow edge tested against a real list rather than asserted on a slide. I screened all twenty-nine against the thesis, which is AI that rebuilds human trust, at pre-seed, in the United States, and I wrote a one-line decision note for every single one of them, including the passes. Twenty-seven were passes, one is worth tracking, and one went into diligence.

The passes did more work than the hit did. Writing twenty-seven reasons in a row made me name the four ways a company can look like this thesis and not be it: trust in machines rather than trust between people, AI as a method rather than as the substance, efficiency dressed up as connection, and AI that spends trust rather than building it. That last group is the one that proves the filter works, because those companies are AI, United States, pre-seed and human-facing, and still wrong. The test I came out of the screen with is one line, and I now apply it before anything else: does this change how two people regard each other, or only how one party regards a machine?

Watch the Adding Deals to Hub video at https://fi.co/guides/2721/legacy_show, add the companies below to Decile Hub trialing at least two methods (manual entry, forwarding a deck or an email to the Hub inbox, importing from a URL or public profile), then replace this bracket with a couple of sentences on which methods you used and which one worked best.]

[BEFORE SUBMITTING - CONTACT. Reach out to each company below to open the conversation for the deal memo set, then replace this bracket with a couple of sentences on who you contacted, what you said, and what came back. "No response yet" is a real answer inside a one-week window and the sprint guidance says so outright.]

One thing I would rather state plainly than paper over. The set asks for three startups currently fundraising, and this channel produced one company I would actually write a check into and one more worth tracking, not three. I would rather submit one real name and say where the other two are coming from than pad the list with companies I have not screened. The two channels I am running next are Grid110's current cohort, where the founders are by definition raising or about to be, and Material Change's portfolio and alumni, which is the most thesis-aligned of my three ecosystems by name alone. [ADD THE THIRD NAME, AND ANY FURTHER NAMES, HERE ONCE THOSE TWO CHANNELS PRODUCE THEM.]

The pipeline as it stands:

- Glacis. https://glacis.io. Pre-seed: $575,000 raised from Geoff Ralston's Safe Artificial Intelligence Fund, Mighty Capital, Sourdough Ventures, Lionheart Ventures, AI House and the AI2 Incubator, with a seed planned for later in 2026, so the window is opening rather than open. What they do: a flight recorder for enterprise AI, sitting at the point where a model acts and producing a cryptographically signed receipt for every governed action, so that a third party can verify what the system actually did without having to trust the vendor or the system that generated the record. How I found them: Plug and Play Seattle Batch 3, my own alumni network, surfaced in the twenty-nine-company screen above. Why I think it is a good deal: existing monitoring answers "did it work," Glacis answers "did it follow our rules," and it hands that answer over as a receipt an auditor, a patient, or a rejected applicant can actually rely on. That is the narrow line my thesis draws, which is that the product has to give something to the person on the receiving end rather than only protect the machine. The team maps onto the buyer unusually well for pre-seed: a psychiatrist of nearly two decades who was medical director at Cognoa, an operator who has taken deep technology into regulated markets before, and a CTO who spent nineteen years at Microsoft, most recently on the Azure AI Foundry team. They also publish their format, OVERT 1.0, as an open standard with an open-source SDK, which is a bet that the category forms around them rather than a pure product bet.
- Casium. casium.com. Seed, $5,000,000 raised, which is past my entry point, so this is a tracking entry rather than a live deal and I am listing it as one. What they do: AI plus attorney oversight to cut work-visa filings from months down to days. How I found them: Plug and Play Seattle Batch 2, in the same screen. Why it is on the list anyway: visas decide who gets to belong, which is the closest thing to my thesis in the whole batch, and I want the conversation on record before I decide whether filing automation sold to employers is the thesis or is adjacent to it.

Scoring my first three sprints, one to five, with no threes:

- Sprint 1, Orientation and Investment Thesis: 4. The thesis is specific in all three variables, AI rebuilding human trust at pre-seed in the United States, it names a real dealflow edge in Plug and Play, Grid110 and Material Change rather than claiming a generic network, and since submitting it I have closed the hole I flagged in it by writing an anti-thesis out of twenty-nine companies I actually screened rather than out of my head, which gives the thesis four named categories of near-miss and a one-line test so that it can finally say no; what still keeps it off a 5 is that the edge is asserted without a single name behind it.
- Sprint 2, Venture Fundamentals: 4. The glossary outgrew the assignment and now runs to 249 terms, each with a plain-language definition and its own deep-dive page covering why the term matters, what it looks like in practice and where it goes wrong, with 204 of those terms carrying a worked example with real numbers, all of it published and version-controlled alongside a public diagram of how capital flows through a fund; what keeps it off a 5 is that one answer inside this sprint describes my focus as AI and humanity at pre-seed to seed and argues fund sizing in the first person, and that is not my position.
- Sprint 3, Venture Careers: 2. The thinking is there, that Venture Partner is the real route in and is paid in carry rather than salary, that ecosystem builder comes first with syndicates in parallel, and that the geography answer is being the first call in Seattle rather than the fortieth in San Francisco, but the answers are saved as drafts rather than submitted, the outreach is written and unsent, and the working group feedback is still a placeholder, so scoring it a 4 would be scoring my intentions.

Sprint 3 scored below a 4, so here is what I am fixing before I submit it: sending the outreach messages, listening to the two podcast episodes the reflection is written from, verifying the names and profile URLs I deliberately left unverified, and replacing the working group placeholder with what people actually said. I also checked every link in my public notebook, 54 unique URLs across the repository and the site. Fifty of them return cleanly. Three of the remaining four are automated-traffic blocks at Carta, Cooley GO and LinkedIn that open normally in an incognito window rather than dead pages. The fourth is a link to a personal GitHub repository of mine that is not public, and that is the one link in the notebook a signed-out grader genuinely cannot open, so I am either making it public or removing the link before this goes in.

One correction I would rather state plainly than quietly edit. My fund economics answer from Sprint 2 describes my focus as AI and humanity at pre-seed to seed, and it argues in the first person that I should size a fund small enough that a $300 to $500 million exit still returns it. My thesis is AI rebuilding human trust, meaning bridges, community bonds and belonging, at pre-seed, and I am writing personal angel checks today, so fund sizing is something I am learning toward rather than operating now. The reasoning in that answer is not wrong. It is answering a question I do not have yet.

My key learnings from the first half of the program. The one that reorganized how I read a cap table is that being early does not mean being paid first: proceeds run through a distribution waterfall in a strict order, capital back first, then a preferred return of around 8%, then carry, and among preferred shareholders the later rounds are usually paid before the earlier ones. When Kabbage sold, Series F took $161 million, then Series E took $166 million, then D took $50 million, then C took $31 million, leaving $22 million for Series A and B while common shareholders still held roughly 28% of the company. The second is structural: what looks like one venture firm is three entities, a management company, a fund and a general partner, doing deliberately separated jobs, and the separation is the discipline rather than the paperwork. The third is about my own position. I came into this program planning to learn how to run a fund, and I am leaving the first half convinced that the order matters more than the destination, which means angel checks first, then a real track record, then a fund. The fourth I learned by doing rather than by reading, in the last week of the half: a thesis is only a filter once you run it against a list you did not pick. Screening twenty-nine companies produced twenty-seven passes, and it was the passes, not the one hit, that showed me where the edge of my own thesis actually sits. I could not have written that from a desk.
